prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of gamma-ray burst afterglows, which established the cosmological origin of gamma-ray bursts

statement.case_for: B025 is the clearest case on the shortlist of a discovery in the sense I care about: nature gave us a thirty-year puzzle, and a specific instrumental step (BeppoSAX arcminute X-ray localisation within hours) followed by optical and radio counterparts and redshifts settled it. Gamma-ray bursts turned out to be cosmological, among the most luminous events known, tied to the deaths of massive stars and later to neutron-star mergers. That has an existential dimension, since it tells us how stars die and probes the early universe. Nearly three decades of independent confirmation, thousands of afterglows and a stable interpretation make this fully mature, and the experiment-plus-follow-up split among Costa, Frontera and Kulkarni is natural. After reading the other ballots I keep it first, partly because it is the one candidate where a decisive observation, not a method or a platform, is the achievement.
statement.case_against: The credit is genuinely contested. The BeppoSAX team gave the localisation, but the optical afterglow and the first redshift came from ground-based groups, and van Paradijs (deceased) and others, for example Groot, Djorgovski and the radio and redshift teams, cannot be represented in three names. Only two colleagues ranked B025 at all, so it has the thinnest support among my favoured candidates, and a committee may judge that it is astronomy and belongs to a different prize culture. The three-person limit may force an arbitrary cut among decisive people, which would be a real problem for a prize that should name the people behind the discovery.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B024) first as a measurement instrument that redefines what can be measured, with Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's systematics work as a clean two-person credit, and notes the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes are only a modest overlap.
responses.response: I respect the clean attribution, and I ranked B024 sixth myself, so I am not dismissing it. My reservation is the one Kroll flags: the impact on fundamental physics so far consists of limits, not a discovery, and the headline payoff, the redefinition of the second, is still pending. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems sit very close in the prize history. I would be more persuaded if a clock comparison found a variation of constants or a dark-matter signal. Until then I see B024 as an outstanding precision achievement but a weaker discovery than an afterglow, which nature simply delivered to us.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B052) first as a detector-driven opening of a new observational window and B025 second, while noting that a single credited name for IceCube may not reflect who built the instrument.
responses.response: We agree on how the two astrophysics candidates should be valued, and I ranked them in the same order of pairing, opposite orientation. Where I differ is maturity and attribution. The diffuse flux is solid, but source identification beyond TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 is still at modest significance, and the Galactic-plane result is recent. A Halzen-only prize also leaves out the engineers and collaboration leaders, as Pearce says. For B025 the interpretive questions were closed years ago. I would keep B052 as the natural next candidate once source astronomy matures, and I do not think the committee should hurry it ahead of a result that has had thirty years to be tested.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B021) first as a theory-plus-experiment story with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and says the central discovery of correlated phases is robust despite the open pairing question.
responses.response: I agree that B021 is a real discovery in which experiment confirmed a prediction, and I ranked it fourth. But I take the point of Mehlig and Olsson that the field is still young and the nature of the superconductivity is unresolved, and I would not call it settled enough to rank above something with decades of testing. I also have a qualification on credit: Cao's role as first experimental author is not representable here, and the three-name cut then falls on Bistritzer, whose role is real. If the committee prefers a condensed-matter prize this year, I would support MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, but I would not make it the default.

uncertainties: How the committee should divide credit between the BeppoSAX team and the ground-based optical, radio and redshift groups, given only three names and the death of van Paradijs.
Whether colleagues who ranked it low regard B025 as astronomy rather than physics, or find the satellite-plus-follow-up credit too diffuse.
Whether a two-part prize pairing the GRB discovery with IceCube is feasible, since the credited names total four people.
Whether the maturity of IceCube source identification will improve enough in the next few years to change my ordering.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: none of the shortlisted candidates or credited individuals are among my known connections (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet, the Uppsala string group), and my own research in string theory and dark bubble cosmology does not touch these entries.
